message.content: The last common ancestor of a lion (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and a zebra (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) is the most recent common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). That ancestor lived roughly 160 million years ago during the late Jurassic/early Cretaceous period.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. We need to answer with the common ancestor. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals but belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their last common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? Actually, lion is a cat (Felidae), zebra is an equid (Equidae). Both are mammals, but they diverged earlier. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the last common ancestor of marsupials and eutherians? Wait, lion is a placental mammal (eutherian). Zebra is also a placental mammal. So their last common ancestor is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which is the last common ancestor of all eutherians. That ancestor lived about 160 million years ago. But maybe we can give a more precise answer: The last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. That ancestor lived around 70-80 million years ago. But the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~160 million years). So the answer could mention that the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which existed around 160 million years ago.

We should provide a concise answer. No code needed.
